title: Corporate Bonds and Credit
intro: When a company borrows, the lender takes on the chance that it won't pay. Corporate bonds pay a higher yield than government bonds to compensate, and the size of that extra yield, the credit spread, is the market's price of default risk. This page covers ratings, spreads, what happens in default, and where bonds sit in a company's capital structure.

blocks.text: Rating agencies, chiefly S&P, Moody's and Fitch, grade issuers by their chance of default. The scales line up roughly like this:

blocks.source:
S&P / Fitch   Moody's      Meaning
AAA           Aaa          highest quality (very few companies; Microsoft, Johnson & Johnson)
AA            Aa
A             A
BBB           Baa          lowest investment grade
--------------------------------- investment grade above, high yield below
BB            Ba           speculative
B             B
CCC, CC, C    Caa, Ca, C   substantial risk; near default
D             -            in default

blocks.text: Investment grade (BBB−/Baa3 and above) is what many pension funds, insurers and bond funds are allowed to own. Below it is high yield, also called junk. A bond cut from BBB to BB is a fallen angel, and forced selling often pushes its price below fair value. Historically the average yearly default rate has been well under 0.1% for A-rated issuers and around 4% for single-B, with cumulative five-year rates rising steeply further down the scale. Ratings lag the market and have failed badly before (AAA-rated mortgage securities in 2007-08), so treat them as a starting point.

A corporate bond's yield is the government yield for that maturity plus a spread, quoted in basis points (bp; 100 bp = 1%). The spread pays for expected default losses, for the uncertainty about them (a risk premium), and for poorer liquidity. A rough guide to expected loss:

blocks.caption: PD is the yearly probability of default and R the recovery rate.

blocks.text: With a 2% default probability and 40% recovery, expected loss is 1.2% a year; a spread of 4% would leave 2.8% as compensation for risk and illiquidity. Historically spreads have been more than enough to cover average losses in investment grade, which is the credit risk premium, but they widen sharply in recessions: US high-yield spreads went from about 3% to over 19% in late 2008 and above 10% in March 2020.

blocks.alt: A stack showing who gets paid first when a company fails: secured debt at the top, then senior unsecured bonds, subordinated bonds, preferred stock and common stock at the bottom, with typical recovery rates falling and risk and expected return rising down the stack.
blocks.caption: Who is paid first. Each layer is paid in full before the next gets anything (the absolute priority rule), so recovery falls and risk rises down the stack.

items: Secured debt (bank loans, secured bonds) has a claim on specific assets. Typical recovery in default has been 60 to 80%.
Senior unsecured bonds: the usual corporate bond; average recovery around 40%.
Subordinated (junior) bonds rank below senior debt and recover less.
Preferred stock, then common stock, which usually gets nothing.
Covenants restrict the borrower: limits on more debt, on paying dividends, or on selling assets. High-yield bonds and loans have more of them; 'covenant-lite' loans have few.
Convertible bonds can be swapped for a set number of shares; they pay a lower coupon in exchange for that option on the stock's upside.
Floating-rate loans (leveraged loans) have coupons that reset with short-term rates, so little interest-rate risk but full credit risk.

Contingent convertibles (CoCos, AT1 bonds) are bank bonds that convert to equity or are written off when the bank's capital falls. Credit Suisse's AT1 bonds were written to zero in 2023 while its shareholders kept something, a reminder to read the terms.
Leverage: net debt / EBITDA; interest coverage: EBIT / interest (see Reading Financial Statements).
Free cash flow against debt due in the next few years (the maturity wall).
The business's stability: a utility can carry more debt than a cyclical miner.
Market signals: the bond spread and the credit default swap (CDS) price, which is the yearly cost of insurance against the issuer's default.

Merton's structural model (1974) treats equity as a call option on the firm's assets with the debt as the strike; the distance between the asset value and the debt, in units of asset volatility (distance to default), drives the default probability. Moody's KMV commercialized it.

blocks.text: High-yield bonds behave partly like stocks: they fall in recessions, just when you want your bonds to hold up. Many portfolios therefore keep their 'safe' allocation in government and high-grade bonds and treat high yield as part of the risky side, if they hold it at all.

blocks.title: Is the spread enough?
blocks.text: A B-rated bond yields 8.0% when the Treasury of the same maturity yields 4.2%. You estimate a 4% yearly default probability and 40% recovery. What is the expected loss, and what is left as a risk premium?
solution: About 1.4% a year is left as compensation for risk and illiquidity, before costs.

blocks.title: Implied default probability
blocks.text: A bond trades at a spread of 2.5% over government bonds. If you assume recovery of 40% and the whole spread pays for expected loss, what yearly default probability does the market imply?
solution: $PD \approx \text{spread}/(1 - R) = 0.025/0.6 \approx 4.2\%$ a year. This is a 'risk-neutral' probability, and real-world default rates are usually lower because part of the spread is a risk premium.

blocks.title: Recovery and ranking
blocks.text: A company with \$500 million of assets left after bankruptcy costs owes \$300 million of secured loans and \$400 million of senior unsecured bonds. How much do the bondholders recover per dollar, and what do shareholders get?
solution: Secured lenders are paid in full (\$300 million), leaving \$200 million for \$400 million of bonds: 50 cents on the dollar. Shareholders get nothing.
blocks.answer: 50 cents per dollar; nothing for shareholders
